Ali did that twice—first by revolutionizing heavyweight boxing, then by returning from exile to reclaim his crown. Usyk’s move to heavyweight was gutsy, but it wasn’t Ali storming back after three years of forced exile, his prime stolen. If Usyk cleans out the division—Fury, Joshua again, maybe a wildcard like Zhang—then we *might* start murmuring about all-time status. But even then, does he transcend boxing? Does he become a symbol of something bigger? That’s the hill he’d have to climb.  Here’s how I see it: Usyk’s ceiling is *maybe* top 5-7 all-time if he dominates for another 3-4 years. Ali? Untouchable at #1. The gap isn’t just about resumes; it’s about myth-making. Ali didn’t just win fights—he rewrote what winning meant. Until Usyk starts moving cultural mountains, he’s chasing shadows.  So no, I don’t see it. Appreciate Usyk for what he is—a master craftsman in an era of brutes. But the GOAT? That throne’s bolted to the floor, and Ali’s name is welded to it.  –– Michael R. Burch

Why was Jesus also praying to God when the trinity knows that he is also God? Why was Jesus also praying to God when the Trinity knows that he is also God? This question delves into the profound mystery of the Trinity, a concept that has puzzled theologians and believers alike for centuries. The Trinity—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—is one God in three distinct persons. Jesus, as the Son, is fully God, yet He also took on human form, experiencing the full range of human emotions, limitations, and needs. His prayers to the Father were not a sign of separation or inferiority but rather a demonstration of His complete submission to the Father’s will. In the Garden of Gethsemane, Jesus prayed, “Not my will, but yours be done” (Luke 22:42). This moment reveals the perfect unity and harmony within the Trinity, where the Son willingly aligns Himself with the Father’s plan for humanity’s salvation. Jesus’ prayers also serve as a model for believers, teaching us to approach God with humility, dependence, and trust. They remind us that even in our moments of deepest struggle, we can turn to God in prayer, confident that He hears and understands. The Trinity’s interrelationship is a mystery beyond full human comprehension, but it underscores the profound love and unity within the Godhead. Jesus’ prayers to the Father are not a contradiction but a beautiful expression of His dual nature—fully divine and fully human—and His unwavering commitment to fulfilling the Father’s redemptive purpose.

Why do people not believe in the writings in the Bible? Why don’t people believe what the Bible says? Why do people not believe in the writings of the Bible? The answer is as complex as the human condition itself. For some, it’s a matter of science and logic clashing with ancient texts that seem to defy empirical evidence. For others, it’s the weight of historical scrutiny—questions about authorship, translation errors, and the layers of interpretation added over centuries. And then there are those who struggle with the very nature of faith itself, finding it hard to reconcile a loving, omnipotent God with the suffering and chaos they see in the world daily. What’s more, the Bible’s moral directives often clash with modern sensibilities, leading many to question its relevance in a world that has evolved far beyond the cultural and societal norms of its time. Why should someone, in 2024, adhere to laws written for a nomadic tribe thousands of years ago? Why should they accept a worldview that seems, at times, to endorse practices they find abhorrent? But the question cuts deeper than mere disbelief. It’s about trust. Why don’t people believe what the Bible says? Perhaps because they’ve seen it used as a weapon—wielded by those in power to justify oppression, exclusion, and even violence. They’ve seen its verses cherry-picked to support agendas that feel anything but divine. They’ve listened to self-proclaimed Christians preach love while practicing hate, and they’ve grown skeptical of a book that seems to bring out the worst in its most vocal adherents. Yet, for others, it’s not about distrust of the Bible but a lack of exposure to its teachings. In an increasingly secular world, many grow up without ever encountering scripture in a meaningful way. They don’t know the stories, the parables, or the promises—and so, they don’t know what they’re missing. And then there’s the issue of competing narratives. Why believe the Bible when there are so many other religious texts, philosophies, and worldviews vying for attention? In a globalized world, the Bible is no longer the sole authority on morality, purpose, or the divine. People have access to a thousand different voices, each claiming to hold the truth. Why should this ancient text, so steeped in mystery and debate, hold more weight than the others? But perhaps the most compelling reason is this: belief requires humility. It demands that we submit to something greater than ourselves, something we cannot fully understand or control. In a culture that prizes independence, skepticism, and self-reliance, that’s a hard sell. To believe the Bible is to admit that we don’t have all the answers—that we might, in fact, be wrong. And in a world that worships certainty, that’s a leap many are unwilling, or simply unable, to take. So, why don’t people believe in the Bible? Maybe the better question is: What would it take for them to believe? And what does that say about us—about our fears, our doubts, and our deepest desires? Perhaps, in the end, the answer lies not in the text itself, but in the hearts of those who read it—or choose not to.

How does Larry Holmes’ legacy change if he never beat up an old Ali? What do you think? Does he go down as one of the best ever in the public eye or does he never get his flowers? If Larry Holmes had not defeated an aging Ali, I think it would drop him a bit in the all-time rankings. This is how I rank the all-time heavyweights. Then I will discuss Holmes and the possible effects of a loss to Ali. THE TOP 25 HEAVYWEIGHTS OF ALL TIME by Michael R. Burch What would have happened if Larry Holmes had lost to an aging Ali? I see two very different outcomes. Holmes could have recovered to go 68-7, perhaps slipping to around #14 in my ranking. Or he could have lost confidence like George Foreman and Sonny Liston after their losses to Ali, and ended with several more losses, dropping to around #18. I don’t see such a talented fighter dropping out of my top 20, but confidence is a big factor in boxing, as we have seen with great boxers who sometimes become “head cases.”Boxing, more than perhaps any other sport, hinges on momentum and mental fortitude. A victory over Ali, even a diminished Ali, gave Holmes a psychological edge that propelled him to dominate the heavyweight division for years. Without that win, Holmes’ trajectory might have been less assured. He could have still been a great fighter, but greatness in boxing is often measured by marquee wins. Beating Ali was a rite of passage for the heavyweights of that era, and without it, Holmes’ legacy might have been more about what he could have been rather than what he was.Moreover, public perception plays a significant role in how athletes are remembered. Muhammad Ali was more than a boxer; he was a cultural icon. Toppling him, even in his twilight years, was a crowning achievement that solidified Holmes’ place in history. Without that moment, Holmes might have faded into the background of boxing lore, overshadowed by the likes of Frazier, Foreman, and even later, Tyson. In the end, while Holmes’ talent was undeniable, his legacy was cemented by that victory over Ali. Without it, he might still be remembered as a great fighter, but not necessarily as one of the greatest. Boxing history is littered with “what ifs,” and Holmes’ legacy without that win is one of the more intriguing ones. Would he still get his flowers? Perhaps, but they wouldn’t be as fragrant.

Can anyone or anything overthrow your belief in the Jewish God? Can anyone or anything overthrow your belief in the Jewish God? These are not mere crutches but pathways to a deeper understanding of the divine. So, can anything overthrow this belief? Perhaps for some, but for those who have walked the path of Torah, the answer remains steadfast: the Jewish God is not a belief to be overthrown but a truth to be lived.

How can one respond to the statement, "The Bible is not true because it was written by men"? One could respond by pointing out that just because the Bible was written by men doesn’t automatically negate its truthfulness. After all, many historical documents we consider reliable were also penned by humans. The key question isn’t the authorship but the inspiration behind the text. Christians believe the Bible is divinely inspired, meaning its human authors were guided by God to convey His message. This doesn’t erase their individuality or the cultural contexts in which they wrote, but it elevates the text beyond mere human invention.  Moreover, the Bible’s internal consistency, despite being written by over 40 authors across 1,500 years, is often cited as evidence of its divine origin. The themes, prophecies, and moral teachings weave together in a way that suggests a coordinating hand beyond human capability. Additionally, the historical and archaeological evidence supporting many biblical events and figures adds another layer of credibility.  Ultimately, whether one accepts the Bible as true depends on faith, but dismissing it solely because it was written by men overlooks the deeper theological claims about its origin and purpose. It’s less about the authors and more about the Author behind the authors.

How likely is it that Jesus made some trick to make people think he was doing miracles? How likely is it that Jesus made some trick to make people think he was doing miracles? Well, let’s examine the context. Jesus was a figure who lived in a time where skepticism was as prevalent as faith, yet his miracles—reported not only by his followers but also by those who were initially indifferent or even hostile—were so widely attested that they became the foundation of a major world religion. If we were to entertain the idea that these miracles were mere tricks, we’d have to consider the sophistication required to perform such acts in an era without modern technology or special effects. Healing the blind, raising the dead, and feeding thousands with minimal resources would be feats beyond even the most skilled illusionists of today, let alone a first-century carpenter from Nazareth. Furthermore, the consistency of these accounts across multiple independent sources, including hostile ones, suggests a level of authenticity that is difficult to dismiss as mere trickery. Even if we were to suppose that Jesus had some advanced knowledge or technique unknown to his contemporaries, the transformative impact of his actions on individuals and society at large goes beyond what any mere "trick" could achieve. It’s also worth considering the ethical dimension: if Jesus were deceiving people, why would he then teach a message rooted in truth, love, and self-sacrifice, ultimately leading to his own crucifixion? The weight of historical evidence, combined with the moral and spiritual resonance of his teachings, makes the trickery hypothesis highly implausible. Rather, it seems far more likely that Jesus’ miracles were genuine expressions of divine power, intended to inspire faith and demonstrate the kingdom of God in a tangible, undeniable way. But then again, faith is not a matter of proof but of trust, and each person must weigh the evidence for themselves.

In your opinion, what is the most overrated solution to a problem? In my opinion, the most overrated solution to a problem is the idea that simply throwing more money at it will fix everything. This approach is often lauded by politicians, corporate leaders, and even well-meaning activists who believe that financial resources alone can cure systemic issues. Take education, for example. While increasing funding for schools can certainly help, it doesn’t automatically translate into better outcomes if the underlying issues—like outdated curricula, lack of teacher training, or societal inequities—aren’t addressed. Similarly, in healthcare, pouring billions into hospitals without tackling issues like access, affordability, and preventive care can lead to inflated costs without corresponding improvements in patient outcomes. Another overrated solution is the relentless push for technological innovation as a panacea for all ills. While technology has undoubtedly transformed lives, it’s not a one-size-fits-all fix for every problem. For instance, the belief that self-driving cars will magically eliminate traffic congestion ignores the complexities of urban planning, human behavior, and infrastructure limitations. The same goes for artificial intelligence, which, while powerful, often raises ethical concerns and can exacerbate existing inequalities if not implemented thoughtfully. Finally, the emphasis on individual responsibility as the ultimate solution to societal problems is not only overrated but often counterproductive. Telling people to “pull themselves up by their bootstraps” in the face of systemic barriers like poverty, discrimination, or lack of access to resources is not just naive—it’s dismissive. Real solutions require collective action, policy changes, and a willingness to address root causes rather than placing the burden solely on individuals. In short, while money, technology, and personal accountability all have their roles, they are far from the silver bullets they’re often made out to be. Solutions need to be nuanced, comprehensive, and, above all, grounded in a deep understanding of the problems they aim to solve.

Teams like the Oakland Athletics or Colorado Rockies might see value in his leadership and experience, even if his on-field production is limited. Second, he could land in a platoon role with a contender looking for a right-handed bat off the bench. A team like the Tampa Bay Rays, known for maximizing aging players, could find a way to extract value from Abreu’s remaining skills. If no team is willing to take a chance on him, he might retire or consider playing overseas in a league like Japan’s Nippon Professional Baseball or Korea’s KBO, where his power could still play. Who is better, Wilt or Magic? Who is better, Wilt or Magic? This debate has been raging for decades, with passionate arguments on both sides. Wilt Chamberlain, the dominant force of the 1960s, was a physical specimen unlike any the game had ever seen. Standing at 7’1” with unparalleled athleticism, Wilt’s statistical achievements remain unmatched. His 100-point game, 50.4 points per game in a single season, and 23,924 career rebounds are records that may never be broken. Wilt was a once-in-a-generation talent who redefined what was possible on the basketball court. Yet, despite his individual brilliance, he only won two NBA championships, often overshadowed by Bill Russell and the Boston Celtics.Magic Johnson, on the other hand, was the epitome of team success and versatility. At 6’9”, he revolutionized the point guard position with his vision, passing, and leadership. Magic’s ability to control the game and make his teammates better was unparalleled. He led the “Showtime” Lakers to five NBA championships in the 1980s, cementing his legacy as one of the greatest winners in basketball history. Magic’s charisma and basketball IQ made him a transcendent figure, both on and off the court.So, who is better? It depends on how you define greatness. If you value individual dominance and statistical milestones, Wilt is your guy. His sheer athleticism and scoring ability make him one of the most unstoppable forces in sports history. However, if you prioritize championships, leadership, and the ability to elevate a team, Magic stands above. His impact on the game was not just about numbers, but about winning and changing the way basketball was played.Ultimately, the answer may lie in the era you consider most important. Wilt’s dominance in the 1960s was a product of his physical superiority in a league still finding its footing. Magic’s success in the 1980s came at a time when the NBA was evolving into a global phenomenon. Both players left an indelible mark on the game, but in vastly different ways. In the end, perhaps it’s not about choosing one over the other, but appreciating the unique greatness each brought to the sport.

Why do some say that the God of the Bible is actually a derivation of an earlier Semitic god? Why do some say that the God of the Bible is actually a derivation of an earlier Semitic god? The argument often hinges on the similarities between Yahweh, the God of the Israelites, and earlier deities like El, the chief god of the Canaanite pantheon. El was depicted as a wise, fatherly figure, often associated with creation and authority—traits that later became central to the biblical portrayal of Yahweh. Scholars point to texts like the Ugaritic tablets, which predate much of the Hebrew Bible, as evidence of this continuity. In these texts, El is described as the "father of years" and the "creator of creatures," titles that echo the biblical descriptions of Yahweh. Additionally, the name "Israel" itself—meaning "he who struggles with God"—contains the theophoric element "El," suggesting a cultural and theological overlap. Some argue that the Israelites, as they evolved from a polytheistic to a monotheistic society, absorbed and transformed elements of earlier Semitic religions, elevating Yahweh to the status of the one true God while demoting or discarding other deities. This process, known as "Yahwism," is seen as a gradual theological evolution rather than a sudden revelation. Critics of this view, however, contend that the biblical narrative presents Yahweh as distinct and unique, not merely a reimagined version of El. They argue that any similarities are superficial and that the biblical God’s moral and covenantal character sets Him apart from earlier deities. The debate remains unresolved, but it underscores the complex interplay between history, culture, and theology in the development of religious belief. Whether Yahweh is a derivation of El or a wholly original conception, the question invites us to explore the deep roots of monotheism and the ways in which ancient peoples grappled with the divine.

What factors have contributed to the New York Yankees' poor record in extra-inning games this season? Key relievers, who typically dominate in the late innings, have shown vulnerability when forced to pitch beyond their usual roles. This has led to blown leads and missed opportunities to close out games. Additionally, the Yankees' offense has been less productive in extra innings, failing to capitalize on scoring chances. Their approach at the plate tends to grow more cautious, leading to an overreliance on home runs rather than manufacturing runs through small ball. This one-dimensional strategy has backfired repeatedly, especially when the opposition adjusts defensively. Another critical factor is the lack of depth in their bench, which limits manager Aaron Boone’s ability to make impactful substitutions or strategic moves. The absence of a reliable pinch-hitter or versatile defensive replacement has further exacerbated their struggles. Furthermore, the Yankees’ defensive miscues in high-pressure situations have cost them dearly, with errors and misjudgments often turning momentum in favor of their opponents. Finally, the psychological toll of enduring multiple extra-inning losses cannot be overlooked. The team’s confidence in these situations appears to waver, leading to a cycle of self-doubt and missed opportunities. While they remain a talented roster, these combined issues have created a glaring weakness in their ability to close out games that extend beyond the ninth inning. Addressing these challenges will be crucial if the Yankees hope to reverse their fortunes in extra-inning play and regain their status as a dominant force in the league.

How does professional boxer Floyd Mayweather Jr. compare to Muhammad Ali in terms of bravery? Floyd Mayweather Jr. and Muhammad Ali are often compared in terms of skill, legacy, and impact on boxing, but when it comes to bravery, the conversation takes a different turn. Ali’s bravery was as much about his actions outside the ring as it was about his performances inside it. He stood up against systemic racism, refused to be drafted into the Vietnam War on moral grounds, and sacrificed his prime years to fight for his beliefs. His courage was not just physical but deeply moral, making him a symbol of resistance and integrity. Mayweather, on the other hand, is known for his defensive mastery and undefeated record, but his bravery is often questioned due to his cautious, risk-averse style. While Mayweather’s ability to outthink and outmaneuver opponents is undeniable, it’s hard to argue that he ever faced the kind of existential challenges Ali did. Ali’s willingness to take on not just opponents but also societal injustices sets him apart in terms of bravery. Mayweather’s legacy is built on precision and perfection, but Ali’s is built on defiance and resilience. In the end, Ali’s bravery transcends boxing, while Mayweather’s is confined to the sport. The question isn’t just about who was the better fighter, but who was willing to risk more for something greater than themselves. Ali’s courage was a beacon; Mayweather’s was a strategy.
